title: A Quorum on Main Avenue
body:
Five times this summer, the city of Brookings has issued nearly the same sentence: Downtown at Sundown runs Thursday evening on Main Avenue, at least four City Council members may attend, and no official business will be conducted. July 30. August 6. August 13. August 20. August 27. The wording barely changes. Read together, the five notices form something unusual: a small bureaucratic liturgy, repeated weekly, announcing in advance that nothing is going to happen.

It would be easy to file this under civic trivia, the kind of item that exists only to be skimmed past on the way to the county road closures. But the repetition itself is worth sitting with, because it says something true and slightly strange about how democracy works in a town the size of Brookings, where the distance between “the government” and “everyone else” is often about the length of a block of Main Avenue on a summer evening.

The notices exist because of open meetings law, the general principle, codified in South Dakota and nearly every other state, that a quorum of an elected body cannot discuss public business outside of a properly noticed meeting. The law was written with a particular image in mind: officials in a back room, a deal struck over coffee, decisions made before the public ever gets a seat at the table. It is a Watergate-era instinct, formalized into statute, meant to prevent power from doing its real work somewhere other than where citizens can watch.

Downtown at Sundown is about as far from a smoke-filled room as a public gathering can get. It is food trucks and folding chairs, kids with balloon animals, a band on a temporary stage. And yet, because at least four of Brookings' council members might plausibly be standing within earshot of each other at the same street festival, the law technically applies. So the city does the responsible, slightly absurd thing: it tells the public, in advance and in writing, that yes, you may see a majority of your council members enjoying kettle corn together, and no, this does not constitute a meeting.

There is something almost comic about the excess here. A different city, a bigger one, would never bother. In a city of a few hundred thousand, the odds of four council members ending up at the same summer concert are low enough not to worry about, and even if it happened, nobody would think to ask. Brookings is small enough that the coincidence is not just possible but expected, week after week, all summer. The notice is not overcaution so much as an honest description of scale: this is a town where the people who govern it and the people they govern share the same six blocks of downtown on a Thursday night.

That proximity is usually described, correctly, as one of the advantages of small-town life. It's also the thing that makes the mechanics of accountability slightly more delicate here than in a state capital. When power and the public share a physical footprint this small, the safeguards meant to keep them separate start to look, on paper, almost fussy. A five-week string of nearly identical disclaimers can read like institutional throat-clearing. But the alternative, a city that simply stopped noticing when its council might gather in public, would be a quieter kind of failure. The value of the notice isn't in what it prevents (nothing was going to happen at Downtown at Sundown regardless) but in what it keeps alive as a habit: the assumption that residents are owed a heads-up any time the appearance of collective power shows up in a public space, even a folksy one.

There's a second, less legal reading available too. The quorum notice is really a map of where the town's elected officials will be standing on a given Thursday. In a media environment saturated with meetings that happen behind screens and packets nobody reads, Downtown at Sundown offers the opposite: a fully public, fully informal encounter with the people who set the budget, argue about zoning, and vote on the things that shape Main Avenue itself. The law's job is to make sure that encounter doesn't quietly turn into governing. What it doesn't regulate, and what residents are free to do with it, is what happens if someone walks up to a council member between the food truck line and the band and says something about the crosswalk on 22nd Avenue.

The notice guarantees the evening is legally empty of business. It doesn't have to be empty of consequence. That part is still up to whoever shows up.

title: The Quorum That Wasn't There
body:
Between now and the end of August, Brookings City Hall will issue six separate public notices warning that a majority of the City Council might be in the same place at the same time. Five of those notices concern Downtown at Sundown, the Thursday evening concert series on Main Avenue. The sixth concerns Meet State, the annual welcome event for South Dakota State University students. In every case the notice says the same thing: at least four council members may attend, no city business will be conducted, this is not a meeting. It is simply, as the language goes, a heads-up.

Read once, this is bureaucratic housekeeping, the kind of thing that exists because South Dakota's open meetings law defines a quorum by proximity rather than intent. Read six times over six weeks, it starts to look like something else: a town narrating its own transparency so insistently that the notice becomes more visible than the substance it's meant to safeguard.

Consider what else happened on the council's actual agenda during this same stretch. On July 30, the council held a public hearing on leasing city property to a private company, RTI, LLC. It passed the second reading of a budget amendment altering the 2026 city budget. It voted to annex two outlots into city limits, extending Brookings's boundary a little further into the county. It reviewed the 2025 financial audit. These are the decisions that shape what the city taxes, owns, and controls going forward. None of them generated a repeated public notice. None of them recurred weekly across the tenure of a whole summer. They happened once, in the standard Thursday-evening format, filed alongside a proclamation for ADA Day and a first reading on rezoning near Third Addition.

The quorum notices, by contrast, are relentless. Every single Thursday in August, without variation in language, the city reminds residents that council members might be standing near a beer garden. The repetition is not evidence of any particular event's importance. It is evidence of a legal reflex: once a councilmember's attendance at a public gathering becomes routine, the notice must become routine too, regardless of whether anything is actually at stake.

There is a version of this story that is purely comic, a small-town parody of sunshine law where the most heavily documented civic activity of the season is elected officials listening to music. But there's a more serious point underneath it, one that matters for how residents relate to their own government. Open meetings statutes were written to prevent quiet, coordinated decision-making outside the public record, the classic fear being officials working out a deal over coffee before ratifying it later in front of cameras. That fear is legitimate. But the law, applied literally to a city the size of Brookings, cannot distinguish between four council members conspiring in a back room and four council members standing twenty feet apart from each other at a street fair, one buying a bratwurst, another watching a cover band. The statute has no mechanism for scale. It treats a town of thirty-five thousand the way it would treat a much larger municipality where council members genuinely might not otherwise cross paths, where any gathering of four is more likely evidence of intention than coincidence.

In a place like Brookings, the opposite is closer to the truth. Council members turning up downtown on a Thursday night isn't a suspicious convergence, it is what living in a small city looks like. They are there for the same reason everyone else is: because Main Avenue on a summer evening is one of the few places the whole town actually shows up. The notice, technically accurate, misrepresents the nature of the event it's attached to. It frames an ordinary act of civic presence, elected officials being residents among residents, as something requiring legal disclosure.

None of this means the notices should stop. The law is the law, and erring toward disclosure is safer than erring away from it. But it's worth naming what the accumulation of these notices actually communicates to a reader scanning the city's public calendar: that compliance can be performed so thoroughly it becomes its own kind of noise, one that risks drowning out the parts of governance that actually deserve scrutiny. A resident who wants to know what the city intends to do with a leased outlot, or how a fifth budget amendment changes municipal spending, has to sort past a stack of nearly identical notices about a concert series to find it.

Transparency, taken to its logical extreme, doesn't always illuminate. Sometimes it just repeats itself until the outline of what matters gets harder to see. Brookings isn't unique in this, but it is small enough that the pattern shows plainly: the loudest notice on the books this August isn't about a lease or an annexation. It's about the possibility that the council might, like everyone else in town, enjoy a Thursday night out.

title: Brookings Learns to Watch the Wrong Thing
body:
There is a particular kind of civic notice that exists purely as a legal reflex. This week's example: Brookings City Council members may be spotted at the 4-H Achievement Day BBQ at the Dacotah Bank Center on August 6, and again at the Regional Growth Alliance's New Resident BBQ at Hillcrest Park on September 15. Both notices carry the same disclaimer, word for word in spirit: enough members may show up to form a quorum, but no official city business will be discussed or acted upon. It's simply a public notice, required by state open meetings law, so that nobody can later claim officials huddled in a corner making decisions over potato salad.

It's a small, almost comic feature of small-town governance, and it's worth pausing on, because it says something true about how Brookings understands transparency: as a matter of bodies in rooms, not of consequences in motion. The law cares, rightly, that elected officials shouldn't conduct the public's business where the public can't see it. But it enforces that principle by watching for coincidence (four council members at a barbecue) rather than by drawing attention to the places where actual decisions, the kind that reshape a town, get made in meetings that almost nobody outside the agenda packet ever reads.

Consider what else sits on the calendar this same stretch of summer. The Planning Commission meets August 4 to review a preliminary plat for the Legacy Addition, a filing that will set the framework for how an entire section of that development can eventually be built out: street layout, lot configuration, density, the shape of a neighborhood that doesn't yet exist. The County Commission, in special session on July 30, took up Resolution #26-29, a construction and operating permit for a solid waste facility in Brookings County, the kind of infrastructure decision that determines where a region's waste goes and who lives near it for the next several decades. The Board of Adjustment, sitting the same evening as the Planning Commission, is untangling four linked requests on a single property at Lake Hendricks, including an after-the-fact variance, essentially a builder who built first and is now asking the county to bless it retroactively.

None of these carry the same statutory alarm bells as the BBQ notices. There's no requirement that the public be warned, in bold, that consequential decisions might be discussed. They simply appear on an agenda, get their allotted minutes, and pass or fail with whoever happens to be in Room 300 or the Board of Adjustment's chambers that night. The Legacy Addition plat, in particular, deserves more scrutiny than a barbecue disclaimer will ever generate, because once a preliminary plat is approved, the shape of that development is largely locked in. Residents who might have opinions about density, drainage, or street connectivity get their say now, at a hearing most of them don't know exists, or not at all.

This isn't a case against sunshine laws. The instinct behind the quorum notices is sound: officials shouldn't be able to claim a chance encounter as cover for real deliberation. But it's worth noticing how lopsided the resulting picture of transparency becomes. A council member eating a hamburger next to three colleagues generates a formal public notice. A plat that determines the physical form of a new neighborhood generates a line on an agenda. The law has, in effect, taught the town to associate transparency with proximity rather than with stakes. It's easier to legislate against secret quorums than to legislate more people into the room for a variance hearing, so the visible machinery of open government ends up policing the low-risk case with more ceremony than the high-risk one.

Brookings is small enough that this distortion is survivable, for now. A council member at a 4-H barbecue is not going to quietly rezone anything between bites. But the same smallness that makes the BBQ notices almost quaint is exactly what makes the plat approvals and permit resolutions matter more, not less. In a city of this size, a handful of commissioners deciding the framework for the Legacy Addition, or signing off on a solid waste facility's operating permit, are making decisions with an outsized, durable effect on how the town looks and functions for the next generation. The county's Department of Legislative Audit will present its 2025 engagement letter at 9 a.m. on August 4, right around the same hour the Board of Adjustment is untangling the Lake Hendricks variances. Nobody will be required to post a special notice warning residents that this is where the real business of the town happens. Maybe that's the notice worth writing.

title: The Week's Real News Is Hiding in Room 310
body:
Scroll through the Brookings community calendar this week and it reads like a study in democratic indifference. A pizza night at Good Roots Farm sits beside a golf fundraiser, which sits beside a library board meeting, which sits beside a committee weighing whether to recommend a moratorium on a 765-kilovolt transmission line that could reshape the landscape of Brookings County for the next half century. All of it rendered in the same clipped, dutiful prose. All of it granted the same visual weight. A pet parade and a high-voltage power line, filed under the same civic genre.

This is worth pausing on, because the flattening is not an accident of formatting. It is close to the truth of how local democracy actually works, and it puts a real burden on the people it serves.

The Brookings County 765kV Transmission Line Advisory Committee met on August 13 in Room 310 of the County/City Government Center, a room that most residents will never enter and could not locate if asked. The agenda: a presentation on high-voltage transmission infrastructure, discussion of a potential moratorium request, and the restructuring of subcommittees. Sign-in began before the meeting. Anyone could request time to speak on items not listed. The next meeting is September 10.

Nothing about that paragraph announces itself as urgent. Compare it to the language used elsewhere on the same calendar: the Pet Parade lets pets “strut down a runway judged by librarians,” Play Dates offers “an hour of hands-on play and exploration,” the block party promises live music from The Hometown Honeys and a Best Dessert contest. These events are described with warmth because they are, in fact, warm. But the transmission line committee, which may determine whether steel towers and high-voltage cable cross farmland that families have worked for generations, gets the same bureaucratic neutrality as a discussion of Hoopla at the library board meeting.

This is not a failure of the reporting. It is a feature of how municipal and county governance communicates with the public: through notice, not narrative. A meeting notice cannot tell you it matters. It can only tell you when and where, and trust that someone is paying attention.

That trust is increasingly misplaced, and not because Brookings residents are apathetic. The Good Roots pizza nights fill up. The farmers market draws families every Saturday morning for produce and free yoga. The block party on 7th and 8th has grown enough to reach its second annual iteration. People here are perfectly capable of showing up for things. What they show up for tends to be legible: a plate of wood-fired pizza, a dessert contest, a golf scramble for cheerleading scholarships. These are events where the stakes and the pleasures are the same size, and both are immediately obvious.

The 765kV line is a different kind of object. Its consequences are large, diffuse, and delayed. A moratorium discussion in August may not visibly matter until a survey crew shows up on a section line two years from now, or until a neighbor's property value shifts because of an easement nobody remembers being decided. High-voltage transmission corridors are, at the moment, one of the most contested pieces of infrastructure in rural America, tangled up in the renewable energy build-out, in questions of eminent domain, in a decades-long argument about who bears the physical cost of power that gets consumed somewhere else. South Dakota is not a bystander to that argument. It is terrain.

None of this shows up in a two-sentence meeting notice, and it should not have to. The notice's job is procedural, not persuasive. But the procedural neutrality of the calendar means the burden of discernment falls entirely on the reader. Nobody is going to tell a Brookings County resident that Room 310 on a Thursday night matters more than the Sunday pizza line at Good Roots Farm. The system is built so that citizens supply their own hierarchy of attention, and it assumes, perhaps too generously, that they will.

There is something almost admirable in a form of governance that refuses to dramatize itself, that describes a possible moratorium on a major transmission corridor with the same flat affect as a dessert contest. It is democracy declining to manipulate its citizens through urgency. But it only works if enough people already know how to read past the flatness, to recognize that “sign-in begins before the meeting” is sometimes the most important sentence on the page. The next meeting is September 10. The pizza will still be there in October.

title: Quorum, Interrupted: The City Council's Summer of Almost-Meeting
body:
There is a particular genre of civic prose that Brookings has, this summer, elevated nearly to art form: the quorum notice that insists, with the gentle firmness of a librarian shushing a toddler, that nothing is happening here. Four City Council members might be at Meet State on August 21. They might be at Downtown at Sundown on July 30, and again August 6, and 13, and 20, and 27, in a kind of civic residency. And each time, the notice arrives like a chaperone at a dance: yes, they'll be in the room, but no, nothing official will occur. No motions. No votes. Just elected officials, standing near each other, enjoying a bratwurst.

One appreciates the diligence. South Dakota's open meetings law is not interested in vibes; it cares about bodies in space, and if four-sevenths of the council happens to cluster near the same funnel cake stand, the state wants a paper trail proving that clustering isn't legislating. Fair enough. Democracy has been undone by cozier things than a shared appetite for sweet corn. But there is something wonderfully absurd about a town so orderly that it must formally announce, in writing, that its leaders are allowed to have a nice evening without accidentally rezoning anything.

Imagine explaining this to a visitor. “Are they meeting?” No. “Are they doing city business?” No. “Will they be in the same three-block radius on Main Avenue, holding lemonade?” Yes, six Thursdays running. It reads like a fugitive being tailed by his own alibi. The council isn't hiding; it's pre-confessing.

And yet the joke, once you sit with it, has a spine. These notices are the small print of self-government, the unglamorous scaffolding that keeps public trust from getting wobbly. It would be easy, elsewhere, for four officials to “run into each other” at a bar and quietly settle next year's budget between rounds. Brookings instead requires that any such gathering be flagged in advance, like a controlled burn. The result is faintly comic, sure, a summer calendar dotted with disclaimers about the absence of business, but comedy here is doing the work of transparency. The notice is boring on purpose. Boring, in municipal governance, is usually a compliment.

Meanwhile, actual business does grind forward, at actual meetings, with actual votes. On July 30 the council will hold hearings on leasing city land to an outfit called RTI, LLC, and on annexing a couple of outlots that sound like a very small nation seeking UN recognition. There will be budget amendments, zoning first readings, an audit report, and a proclamation for ADA Day. This is the unphotogenic marrow of local government, the stuff that never gets a quorum notice because it's the whole point of the meeting rather than an accidental side effect of a summer stroll. Nobody writes a wistful little paragraph about Resolution 26-041. But it's Resolution 26-041, not the funnel cake, that decides who leases what land and where the sidewalk ends.

Out in Lake Hendricks Township, the Planning and Zoning Commission is wrestling with a rather more concentrated drama: one property, four separate requests, including an accessory building larger than the rules allow and a variance filed after the shed, evidently, was already standing. There's a certain folk-tale quality to the after-the-fact variance, the zoning equivalent of asking forgiveness rather than permission, then discovering the county keeps a very detailed ledger of forgiveness requests. Two-thirds of the board must approve the variances; a simple majority will do for the conditional use permit. Somewhere in Lake Hendricks Township, an accessory building is currently living what lawyers call an “unresolved legal status,” which is a fancy way of saying the shed doesn't know yet if it's allowed to exist.

Set the two storylines side by side and Brookings' civic character comes into focus rather nicely. It is a place that will tolerate a shed built first and justified later, but will not tolerate four council members standing near lemonade without a disclaimer. That is not hypocrisy so much as proportion: the shed affects one lot; the council affects everyone. The paperwork scales to the stakes.

So when Thursday rolls around and Main Avenue fills with music and popcorn smell and, yes, probably a majority-adjacent cluster of your elected representatives, go ahead and enjoy it exactly as intended: as a street party, not a session. The notice has already done the worrying for you. That's rather the point of good government, come to think of it. It should be so quietly competent that the most exciting thing on the agenda is the weather, and the biggest scandal in town is a shed that filed its paperwork late.

title: The Council That Convenes to Convene
body:
There is a particular kind of civic poetry buried in the fine print of a public meeting notice, and this week Brookings has produced a haiku of bureaucratic minimalism worth pausing over. On Tuesday, August 18, at 4:00 p.m., City Council members “may gather” at the Downtown Fire Station. The notice is careful, almost tender, to clarify that no official city business will be conducted. This is, in the parlance of municipal law, a quorum notice only: a legally mandated heads-up that enough elected officials might occupy the same room at the same time to technically constitute a quorum, even though nobody intends to do anything quorum-shaped with it.

Picture it. Five or six people who normally spend their evenings arguing about zoning variances and drainage easements will instead stand around, possibly near a fire truck, saying nothing that counts. It is government as performance art. It is the Marina Abramović of municipal governance: sit in a chair, be present, generate no legislative output. If a council member accidentally proposes an ordinance during this gathering, presumably a bell rings somewhere and the whole thing has to be redone with witnesses.

One is tempted to laugh, and one should, but there's something almost bracing about the honesty of it. So much of public life runs on the fiction that assembling and accomplishing are the same motion, that if enough important people are in a room, something important must be happening. Brookings' notice quietly punctures that fiction. Sometimes people gather just to gather. The law simply insists on being told about it in advance, in writing, with accommodations available for those who need them.

Which makes it a useful lens for glancing at everything else on the community calendar this particular stretch of August, because nearly all of it is the cheerful, purposeful opposite of a quorum notice. Where the council's meeting is gathering minus doing, the rest of Brookings seems determined to prove that doing is best achieved through gathering, loudly and specifically.

Take the Friends of University & Central Historic Neighborhood, hauling out lawn chairs on August 28 for live music from The Hometown Honeys, hot dogs, and a Best Dessert in the Neighborhood contest that will almost certainly end in some bar cookie recipe getting photocopied and passed hand to hand for the next decade. Nobody there needs a quorum. They need a folding table and someone willing to admit their bars have cream cheese in them.

Or the SDSU cheerleaders, teeing off at Edgebrook on August 30 with a shotgun start, which is itself a marvelous phrase suggesting either competitive golf or the opening of a Western, and $380 gets a team eighteen holes, a cart, a meal, and a shot at cash prizes, all in service of funding something that exists purely because a group of young women decided to do backflips in public for the honor of the university. That is doing with a vengeance.

Or BARD's roller derby tournament on the 29th, the first of its kind in the state, eight hours of jammers and blockers at the Outdoor Adventure Center, which will generate more genuine, hip-checking, wheel-burning civic energy in a single afternoon than most quorums manage in a fiscal year.

Even the dogs get in on it. Soggy Doggy at Hillcrest Aquatic Center lets vaccinated, sociable, spayed-or-neutered dogs paddle around a public pool for ninety minutes while their owners stand poolside doing absolutely nothing but watching, which is arguably the one instance all month where non-participation is not just permitted but the entire point.

What emerges, if you squint, is a small argument about what community actually consists of. It is not, mostly, made in rooms where people are legally present but functionally idle, however necessary those notices are for transparency's sake. It is made in the specific, slightly ridiculous, deeply local acts of showing up to do a thing: judge a dessert, sink a putt, skate a jam, dunk a labrador. The quorum notice is honest bureaucracy, and honest bureaucracy deserves credit. But it is the block parties and golf scrambles and wet dogs that are doing the actual work of stitching a town together, one hot dog and one backflip at a time.

So by all means, council members, gather at the fire station and conduct no business whatsoever. Just know that three blocks over, someone is icing a dessert entry, and that, too, is a kind of civic meeting, no minutes required.

title: Brookings Perfects the Art of the Non-Meeting
body:
There is a particular kind of magic trick performed with some regularity in Brookings this time of year, and it goes like this: several members of city government stand in the same place, at the same time, often holding a ceremonial pair of scissors or a novelty-sized shovel, and nothing happens. Officially, that is. Unofficially, quite a lot happens: a skate park opens, a fire station breaks ground, ice cream gets social, a trolley clatters down 5th Street, a block party breaks out on 8th Avenue. But should you consult the public record, you will find the same tidy disclaimer stitched into nearly every one of these gatherings like a warning label on a mattress: “though no official city business will be conducted.”

It's a lovely little incantation, that phrase. Said often enough, it starts to sound like a spell cast to keep a room full of elected officials from accidentally legislating something. And in a sense, that's exactly what it is. When enough members of a city council or a board show up in one location at one time, they risk assembling a quorum, and a quorum under South Dakota's open meetings law is not a casual thing. A quorum has consequences. A quorum needs an agenda, minutes, proper notice. A quorum is basically a meeting wearing government's Sunday clothes, whether it wanted to get dressed up or not.

So instead, Brookings threads a very particular needle this August: council members attend the ribbon cutting for the new Dwiggins-Medary Skate Park, they show up for the fire station groundbreaking the next evening, several make an appearance at the International Ice Cream Social at Good Roots, the Historic Preservation Commission climbs aboard a trolley and later wanders a block party, and at every stop the record insists, gently but firmly, that nobody did any governing. They were merely present. Adjacent to civic life, but not touching it. Like a chaperone at a school dance who agrees, by unspoken treaty, not to actually dance.

Meanwhile, just across town and just a day later, the real business does get done, properly quorumed and dutifully minuted: the City Council will consider malt licenses for Kwik Star and Casino 2000, weigh a preliminary plat for the Legacy Addition, and award bids for next winter's snow removal equipment, because someone, somewhere, has to think about February in August. The Weed and Pest Board will reauthorize the gopher bounty program, a phrase that never stops being delightful and that quietly acknowledges Brookings County's longest-running border dispute is not with any neighboring county but with rodents. The Joint Board of Adjustment will decide, by majority vote, whether a property on 20th Avenue may keep horses, a question with the rare distinction of being both zoning law and pastoral poetry.

What emerges, if you squint at the calendar the right way, is a town that has quietly built two separate categories of togetherness: the kind where officials gather to actually decide things, hemmed in by agendas and public comment limited to three minutes a head, and the kind where they gather simply to be seen having ice cream, admiring a skate ramp, or waving from a trolley, present but professionally inert. It's tempting to read this as bureaucratic hairsplitting, and it partly is. But there's something almost touching about it too: a government taking pains to show up for the fun parts of community life without pretending that showing up is the same as governing it. The gopher bounty gets its vote. The ice cream social does not, and does not need one.

Maybe that's the small thought worth carrying home from a summer stuffed with ribbon cuttings and rezoning requests alike: not every gathering has to produce a decision to be worth attending, and not every decision needs a party. Brookings, admirably, keeps finding ways to have both, one carefully labeled event at a time.
